Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system (TIPS) is described as a computer-mediated communication platform to enable hearing parents to use ASL with their DHH children, emphasizing ASL recommendation aligned with speech, multiple ASL display form-factors, and autonomy support. The focus is on addressing communication, attention, and ethical/technical challenges rather than on entertainment or game-like fun, indicating a primarily utilitarian design with functionality first and play used as a context rather than as a game mechanic.

        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The system is used during parent-child joint tabletop play with physical toys and playground-like activities, where children play freely but within a guided context (toys on a table, monitored interactions, ASL prompts). This corresponds best to semi-structured play rather than fully unstructured play or a formal game with explicit rules.

        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),

reasoning: The system is a communication and learning support tool (TIPS) for ASL during parent-child play, not a game of chance or mixed chance/skill. Outcomes (language learning, communication quality) depend on users’ behavior and interaction, with no randomizing or probabilistic game mechanics described. This aligns best with an entirely skill-based activity rather than any chance-based design.

reasoning: The system (TIPS) is explicitly designed for face-to-face joint play and communication between hearing parents and their DHH children, focusing on parent-child interactions rather than solo use. The platform supports real-time ASL during parent-child joint play and face-to-face interactions, indicating the core activity is inherently social with no described solo mode.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The system is a communication and learning platform (TIPS) for parent-child joint play, not a structured turn-based or phase-based game. Interaction is continuous: parents speak, the system recommends and displays ASL via AR/tablet/glasses in real time, and children interact with toys. There is no mention of turns, steps, or restricted action windows; actions (speech, viewing signs, manipulating objects) occur freely and concurrently, best matching an entirely simultaneous interaction pattern.

No asynchronous or turn-delayed mechanics are described, so the design is best characterized as entirely synchronous.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The system supports joint play between hearing parents and DHH children with a shared tabletop environment and common interaction flow (symmetrical structure), but the roles and capabilities are inherently different: parents receive ASL recommendations aligned with their speech and multiple display options, while children are language recipients and play partners. This mix of shared interaction structure with role-specific functions best fits a design that is both symmetrical and asymmetrical.
